passage: Counsellor's note, 14 March. I'm Elizabeth, the faculty mentor for third-year students, and I met Farida today. Farida's list this week runs to seven items, all marked urgent: two assignments due Friday, aptitude test practice, a mock interview, a mother's call every evening, and a roommate's birthday. Farida has started every item and finished none, and handed me an assignment with half its answers blank. Her hands were shaking a little when she showed me the list. I did not add advice. I asked which two things she could finish well by Friday if the other five had to wait. She sat quietly, then circled the assignments and the call home. We agreed she would tell her roommate she can join for cake only.

qa.q: What day are the two assignments due?
qa.a: The two assignments are due on Friday.

qa.q: What might Farida have been feeling when her hands shook while showing the list?
qa.a: Overwhelmed and anxious: seven things all felt equally pressing, and she had finished none of them.

qa.q: What choice did Farida make, and what did it cost her?
qa.a: Farida circled the assignments and the call home, which meant the aptitude practice, mock interview and most of the birthday plans would wait.

qa.q: How might Farida's roommate feel about hearing that Farida can only join for cake?
qa.a: The roommate may feel a little disappointed at first, but would probably still be glad Farida is coming to the birthday at all.

grounding: A college student treats every task as equally urgent and finishes none until ranking forces something to be left undone.

passage: Sunday, 11 pm. Tonight I wrote everything in red: the two assignments, mock interview prep, the placement form, Amma's call, Simran's farewell dinner, my own laundry. All urgent. I spent three hours hopping between them. The first assignment is half done, the second has a title, the interview prep is a folder with nothing in it. Amma's call was ten rushed minutes and Simran's dinner I skipped altogether, and I feel awful about that. Nothing got my full attention, and everything got a bit of my worry. Maybe if I decide what really matters I have to accept something goes undone. Tomorrow: the first assignment, then Amma, and I'll tell Simran sorry. — Dolma

qa.q: What did Dolma write in red on Sunday night?
qa.a: Dolma wrote the two assignments, mock interview prep, the placement form, Amma's call, Simran's farewell dinner and laundry, all in red.

qa.q: Why does Dolma feel awful at eleven at night?
qa.a: Dolma feels guilty about skipping Simran's dinner and about the rushed call, and also worried because nothing got full attention.

qa.q: What decision does Dolma make for tomorrow?
qa.a: Dolma decides to do the first assignment, then call Amma, and to apologise to Simran, accepting that other things will wait. 🙂

qa.q: How might Simran feel about Dolma missing the farewell dinner?
qa.a: Simran was probably disappointed to see an empty seat, but a clear apology would help Simran understand that Dolma was overloaded, not uncaring.

grounding: A college student marks every task urgent, does none well, and starts to see that ranking means leaving something undone.

passage: The hostel common room at eleven at night was full of laptops. Leela had four tabs open: a lab report due tomorrow, an aptitude test for placements, a birthday video for her roommate and her mother's missed call. Yash leaned over. "Which one's first?" "All of them," Leela said. She typed two lines of the report, then switched to the aptitude test, then to the video. At one in the morning nothing was finished. Yash pulled a sticky note from his pocket. "Rank them, one to four. Four might not happen." Leela stared. She wrote the report first and texted her mother goodnight.

qa.q: How many tabs did Leela have open?
qa.a: Leela had four tabs open.

qa.q: Why did Leela find ranking her tasks so hard?
qa.a: She felt pressured by all four and anxious that leaving one undone meant failing someone, so treating all as equal felt safer.

qa.q: What would you advise Leela to do tomorrow?
qa.a: Rank the tasks by deadline and cost, accept that the lowest one may wait, and finish one before switching.

qa.q: What is it like for Yash to watch Leela switch between tasks?
qa.a: Yash seems patient but concerned; he can see nothing is getting finished, so he offers a simple way to rank them.

grounding: Illustrates a college student treating every demand as equally urgent and learning that ranking means accepting something will wait.

passage:
Dear Manjula akka,
Sorry I missed your call again. This semester everything wants me at once. I have two assignments, placement mock interviews on Fridays, my hostel friends' plans, and Amma's calls every night. I kept saying yes to all of it, and last week I submitted a half-done assignment and fumbled a mock interview. My professor wrote "rushed" in red. It stung.
So I made a list and put numbers next to it. Assignments first, then placements. Friends only on Sunday. Amma's call I'll keep short on weekdays. It feels selfish, but at least things are getting done.
Love,
Kavitha

qa.q: What word did the professor write on Kavitha's assignment?
qa.a: The professor wrote "rushed" in red.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel about ranking the commitments?
qa.a: Kavitha felt uneasy and a bit selfish about it, but relieved that things were finally getting done.

qa.q: What could Kavitha try to keep the plan realistic?
qa.a: Kavitha could review the numbered list each week and tell friends and Amma in advance when there is free time, so the plan feels fair.

qa.q: How might Manjula akka see this letter?
qa.a: Manjula akka may feel understanding and proud that Kavitha is sorting out priorities, even though it means fewer calls.

grounding: Shows a college student juggling assignments, placement prep, friends and family who learns that ranking means leaving something undone.

passage: So you want the story of my second year? Okay. I'm Ayesha, and in second year I believed that if I was a good person, I'd do everything. Coding practice for placements, two group projects, my cousin Arohi's wedding prep, calls home. My calendar looked like a rainbow exploded. I'd start coding, get a wedding message, switch, then feel guilty and open a project. By exam week I had three unfinished things and a cold. My mentor asked me one question: "If only one thing could be excellent this month, which?" Placements. I picked it, told Arohi I'd help at the wedding but not plan it, and I survived.

qa.q: What was the one question Ayesha's mentor asked?
qa.a: "If only one thing could be excellent this month, which?"

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling during those busy weeks?
qa.a: Ayesha felt guilty and overwhelmed, switching from one task to another whenever a message came in.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Ayesha, and why?
qa.a: Choosing placements as the one thing to be excellent and limiting the wedding role gave Ayesha a clear ranking to act on.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Ayesha offers to help but not plan?
qa.a: Arohi might feel a little disappointed at first, but likely grateful that Ayesha was honest about what was possible.

grounding: Illustrates a student treating assignments, placements and family as equally pressing until learning to rank them.

passage:
Monday. Darshan wrote everything on one sticky note: two assignments, aptitude practice for placements, his grandmother's call, a friend's birthday, the college fest meeting. All starred. He started the assignment, then switched to aptitude, then answered the fest group.
Wednesday. At midnight, nothing was finished. The assignment was half done, the aptitude test half done, and he had forgotten his grandmother's call. He felt like he was failing at everything at once.
Saturday. His classmate Ankita sat with him in the canteen. "Rank them. One to six. And something has to be last."
Darshan argued for twenty minutes. Then he wrote: assignment due Monday first, aptitude second, Grandma on Sunday morning. The fest meeting he would skip, and he messaged the group to say so. It felt terrible for about an hour.
By Sunday night, the assignment was submitted. It was the first thing he had finished in a week.

qa.q: What did Darshan decide to skip?
qa.a: The fest meeting.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel on Wednesday at midnight?
qa.a: Darshan felt overwhelmed and defeated, as if he was failing at everything at once.

qa.q: Why did ranking the tasks help, even though something was left out?
qa.a: Ranking let Darshan focus on the assignment first and finish it, accepting that the fest meeting would be left undone.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt as Darshan argued for twenty minutes?
qa.a: Ankita was probably patient but firm, sure that something had to be last for anything to get done.

grounding: Illustrates a college student who treats every task as top priority until ranking them, and leaving one undone, lets him finish something.
